slides.title: What is AI?
slides.text:
AI is short for artificial intelligence. It is technology people build to help computers do things such as recognize pictures, understand words, or answer questions.

Example: A voice helper can hear you ask for a song and try to play the right one.

slides.title: Who makes AI?
slides.text:
AI does not appear by magic. People design the computer programs, choose examples for them to learn from, test them, and improve them.

Example: Just like people build a game, teams of people also build the AI inside some games and apps.

slides.title: How does AI learn from examples?
slides.text:
Many AI systems are trained by showing them lots of examples so they can notice patterns.

Example: If an AI is shown many pictures labeled “cat” and “dog,” it can learn clues that help it guess which animal is in a new picture.

slides.title: Can AI make mistakes?
slides.text:
AI can make mistakes, even when its answer sounds sure. That is why people should check important answers.

Example: An AI might look at a fluffy sheep and accidentally call it a dog.

slides.title: Does AI have real feelings?
slides.text:
AI can use words that sound happy, kind, or sad, but it does not feel emotions the way people do.

Example: An AI can say “I’m happy to help,” but that sentence is generated by a computer system—it is not a real feeling.

slides.title: Can AI help create pictures and stories?
slides.text:
Some AI tools can help create pictures, stories, or ideas when you describe what you want.

Example: You could ask for “a purple dinosaur wearing rain boots,” and an image-making AI could create a picture from that description.

slides.title: Can AI help make music?
slides.text:
Some AI tools can help create music by using patterns learned from lots of sounds and songs.

Example: You might ask for a short, cheerful tune for a pretend birthday party.

slides.title: Can AI answer your questions?
slides.text:
You can ask some AI tools questions and they will try to explain the answer. But AI can sometimes be wrong, so important answers should be checked with a grown-up or trusted source.

Example: You could ask, “Why do we see rainbows?” and then check the answer together.

slides.title: How does AI get better?
slides.text:
AI does not practice by itself like a child learning to ride a bike. People improve AI by training it on more examples, testing it, and giving it feedback.

Example: If an AI keeps confusing cats and foxes, engineers can use more examples to help improve it.

quiz.question: What is AI?
choices: A kind of animal
A computer helper that can listen and talk
quiz.explanation:
AI is technology people build to help computers do tasks that usually need some kind of human-like pattern recognition, such as understanding words or recognizing pictures.

Example: A voice assistant can hear a question and try to answer it, but it is still a computer system—not a living thing.

quiz.question: Can AI feel happy or sad, like you can?
choices: No, it can't really feel things
Yes, exactly like a person
quiz.explanation:
No. AI can use words or voices that sound happy, sad, excited, or caring, but it does not experience those feelings the way a person does.

Example: An AI can say “That’s wonderful!” because that response fits the conversation, not because it actually feels excited.

quiz.question: Who makes AI?
choices: People who build it
It just appears by itself
quiz.explanation:
People make AI. Teams may include programmers, designers, researchers, data experts, and safety testers.

Example: Just as many people work together to make a video game, many people can work together to build an AI tool.

quiz.question: Does AI ever make mistakes?
choices: Yes, it is still learning
No, it is always right
quiz.explanation:
Yes. AI can give the wrong answer or misidentify something, sometimes even while sounding confident.

Example: A picture-recognition AI might see a fluffy sheep and guess that it is a dog.

quiz.question: Can AI help make a song?
choices: Yes, it can make a fun tune
No, AI can never make sounds
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Some generative AI tools can create music from a description or other input.

Example: You could ask for a short, cheerful tune for a pretend birthday party.

quiz.question: How does AI learn what a cat looks like?
choices: By looking at lots of pictures
By magic
quiz.explanation:
People can train an AI using many examples of cats and non-cats. The computer adjusts its internal patterns so it becomes better at telling them apart.

Example: After training on lots of labeled animal pictures, it may correctly recognize a new cat photo it has never seen before.

quiz.question: Can AI help draw a picture for you?
choices: Yes, if you ask it
No, AI can never draw
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Some AI tools can create images from words you type.

Example: You could ask for “a blue elephant riding a skateboard,” and the tool can generate a new picture from that idea.

quiz.question: Can you ask AI a question, like why the sky is blue?
choices: Yes, and it will try to answer
No, AI cannot answer questions
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Some AI tools can answer questions and explain ideas, but they can still make mistakes.

Example: You can ask why the sky looks blue and then check the answer with a grown-up or trusted book.

quiz.question: How does AI get better at things?
choices: By practicing, just like you
It is born knowing everything
quiz.explanation:
AI usually gets better when people train or update it using more data, testing, and feedback. It does not simply practice on its own like a child learning a sport.

Example: If an AI often mixes up foxes and cats, engineers can train and test it on better examples.

quiz.question: Is AI a living animal, like a cat or dog?
choices: No, it's a computer helper
Yes, it's a kind of animal
quiz.explanation:
No. AI is software running on computers. It can respond to people and sometimes seem smart, but it is not alive.

Example: A chatbot can answer “hello,” but it does not eat, sleep, grow, or feel the way an animal does.

slides.title: How can AI understand what you say?
slides.text:
Some speakers, toys, and apps can respond when you talk to them because software helps turn your words into commands.

Example: You might say, “Play my favorite song,” and the device tries to understand what you asked.

slides.title: Where can you find AI?
slides.text:
AI can be used in toys, games, cars, cameras, and many other devices.

Example: A toy car might use sensors and software to notice a wall and turn before it bumps into it.

slides.title: How do apps use AI?
slides.text:
Some apps use AI to help choose what to show you, recognize pictures, or understand what you type.

Example: A video app may suggest another animal video after you watched several animal videos.

slides.title: Why should you ask a grown-up before using AI?
slides.text:
Before using a new AI app, website, or toy, ask a trusted grown-up. They can help check whether it is safe and appropriate for you.

Example: A parent can check whether an app asks for your name, photo, or other information.

slides.title: What information should you keep private?
slides.text:
Some information should stay private when you use an AI tool or any online app.

Example: Do not type your home address, school name, passwords, or phone number unless a trusted grown-up says it is okay.

slides.title: Who works on AI?
slides.text:
Many different people help create and improve AI, including programmers, designers, researchers, teachers, and safety experts.

Example: One person may teach the computer what to look for while another tests whether it makes mistakes.

slides.title: How can AI help around the home?
slides.text:
Some home devices use AI or other smart software to respond to your voice or follow routines.

Example: A smart speaker may help turn on a connected light after you say, “Turn on the lamp.”

slides.title: Why does AI need rules?
slides.text:
AI tools need rules and limits made by people. Those rules can help protect privacy, prevent unsafe actions, and make the tool more useful.

Example: A kids’ app may block certain kinds of content or require a parent’s permission.

slides.title: How do video games use AI?
slides.text:
Games often use AI to control characters that are not being played by a person.

Example: In a racing game, an AI-controlled car can steer around the track and compete with you.

quiz.question: What should you do before using an AI toy?
choices: Ask a grown-up first
Just use it alone
quiz.explanation:
Ask a trusted grown-up first. They can check whether the toy or app is appropriate and whether it asks for personal information.

Example: A parent can help decide if it is okay to turn on the microphone or create an account.

quiz.question: Can AI help a toy car drive by itself?
choices: Yes, AI can help it steer
No, cars can never use AI
quiz.explanation:
Yes. A toy car can use sensors and smart software, including AI in some designs, to notice what is around it and decide how to move.

Example: It might sense a wall and turn before bumping into it.

quiz.question: Do some apps on a phone use AI?
choices: Yes, some apps use AI
No, phones never use AI
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Many apps use AI for things like recommendations, photo tools, speech recognition, or predictions.

Example: A video app may suggest another animal video after you watched several animal videos.

quiz.question: Should you tell an AI your home address?
choices: No, keep that private
Yes, always tell it
quiz.explanation:
No. Your home address is private information and usually is not needed for using an AI tool.

Example: You can ask for help with a story without telling the chatbot where you live.

quiz.question: Can you ask a toy or speaker to play your favorite song?
choices: Yes, some can hear and play music
No, toys can never hear you
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Some smart speakers and toys can turn your spoken request into a command.

Example: You might say the song name out loud and the device will try to play it.

quiz.question: Do grown-ups have jobs building AI?
choices: Yes, that is real, important work
No, AI just appears with no jobs
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Many different jobs help create AI, including programmers, designers, researchers, testers, and safety experts.

Example: One person may build the software while another checks whether it makes mistakes.

quiz.question: Can some AI helpers turn on lights when you talk to them?
choices: Yes, if you say the words
No, lights never listen
quiz.explanation:
Yes. A voice assistant can understand a spoken command and send a signal to a connected smart light.

Example: Saying “turn on the lamp” can switch the lamp on if the devices are connected.

quiz.question: Does even smart AI need to follow rules?
choices: Yes, rules keep everyone safe
No, AI can do anything it wants
quiz.explanation:
Yes. People put rules and limits around AI to make it safer and more useful.

Example: A kids' app may block certain content or require a parent's permission for some features.

quiz.question: Can AI be your teammate in a game?
choices: Yes, it can help characters play with you
No, AI is never in games
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Games can use AI to control computer characters that play with or against you.

Example: An AI teammate might follow you, defend an area, or help complete a game mission.

quiz.question: Why should you ask a grown-up before using something new with AI?
choices: They help make sure it's safe
Grown-ups never know about AI
quiz.explanation:
A trusted grown-up can help check privacy, safety, age rules, and whether the tool is right for you.

Example: They can look at what information the app asks you to share before you start using it.

slides.title: How does AI learn from examples?
slides.text:
Many AI systems are trained on large sets of examples. During training, the computer adjusts itself to get better at spotting useful patterns.

Example: To recognize cats, an AI might study thousands of labeled cat and non-cat pictures.

slides.title: How does AI find patterns?
slides.text:
AI is very good at finding patterns in data. It can use those patterns to make a prediction about something new.

Example: After seeing many photos of dogs, an AI may learn that certain shapes, textures, and features often appear in dog photos.

slides.title: Why can AI make mistakes?
slides.text:
Finding patterns does not mean AI understands everything perfectly. Unusual or confusing examples can still lead to mistakes.

Example: A wolf, husky, or fluffy sheep might confuse an image-recognition system.

slides.title: What should you do when AI gives a wrong answer?
slides.text:
AI can give a wrong answer in a confident-sounding way. A smart user checks surprising or important information instead of trusting it automatically.

Example: If an AI gives a strange fact about a planet, compare it with a trusted science book or reliable website.

slides.title: How is AI different from your brain?
slides.text:
Human brains and AI work very differently. People have lived experiences, emotions, goals, and relationships; AI processes data and produces outputs based on its training and instructions.

Example: An AI can write a birthday message, but it does not know what it feels like to celebrate with a friend.

slides.title: Is a robot the same as AI?
slides.text:
A robot is a physical machine. AI is software that can help a machine recognize, predict, plan, or respond. A robot may use AI, but it does not have to.

Example: A factory robot can follow fixed instructions, while a voice chatbot can use AI without having any robot body.

slides.title: How can AI create pictures, stories, or music?
slides.text:
Generative AI can make new-looking pictures, stories, music, and other content by combining patterns learned during training.

Example: You could ask for a story about a penguin detective on the Moon, and the AI can generate one from your prompt.

slides.title: How can AI recognize objects in photos?
slides.text:
Computer-vision AI can be trained to identify objects in pictures by learning from many examples.

Example: A photo app might recognize that a picture contains a bicycle, a dog, or a tree.

slides.title: Why does training AI take many examples?
slides.text:
Training an AI usually takes lots of data, testing, and repeated adjustments. One example is rarely enough for a system to become reliable.

Example: Engineers may train an image system on thousands or millions of examples before using it in a real product.

quiz.question: How does AI usually learn to recognize things?
choices: By looking at lots of examples and finding patterns
By reading a single instruction book once
quiz.explanation:
Many AI systems are trained on lots of examples so they can learn useful patterns.

Example: A dog-recognition system may study many different dog photos so it can recognize dogs it has not seen before.

quiz.question: True or False: AI never makes mistakes.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation:
False. AI can make mistakes because the patterns it learned may not fit every new situation.

Example: An image system trained on many dogs could still confuse a husky with a wolf.

quiz.question: What's something your brain can do that AI really can't?
choices: Truly understand feelings and have original ideas
Recognize a picture of a dog
quiz.explanation:
People have lived experiences, emotions, relationships, personal goals, and a sense of being in the world. AI processes data and generates outputs without having those human experiences.

Example: AI can write about missing a friend, but it does not actually know what missing someone feels like.

quiz.question: Is a robot the same thing as AI?
choices: Yes, they're identical
No — a robot is a machine; AI is the smart software
quiz.explanation:
No. A robot is a physical machine, while AI is software that can recognize, predict, plan, or respond. Robots can use AI, but not every robot does.

Example: A chatbot can use AI without any robot body at all.

quiz.question: Can AI create new pictures or stories using patterns it learned?
choices: Yes, by mixing patterns it learned
No, AI can only copy things exactly
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Generative AI can produce new-looking content by combining patterns it learned during training and following a prompt.

Example: You could ask for a story about a dragon who becomes a librarian, and the AI can generate a new version of that idea.

quiz.question: What did AI likely study before it can recognize a 'dog' in a photo?
choices: Millions of labeled example photos
Just one single photo of a dog
quiz.explanation:
It was likely trained on many example images, often with labels or other signals that helped it learn which patterns are associated with dogs.

Example: Seeing many breeds, sizes, backgrounds, and poses can help the system work better on new dog photos.

quiz.question: Does AI usually get good at a task instantly, after just one example?
choices: No, it usually needs thousands of examples
Yes, one example is always enough
quiz.explanation:
Usually not. Many AI systems need large amounts of training data, repeated testing, and adjustment before they become reliable.

Example: One photo of one dog would not teach an image system what every kind of dog looks like.

quiz.question: What can happen when AI runs into something unusual, like a fluffy sheep that looks like a dog?
choices: It can guess wrong because they look similar
This can only ever confuse a human, never AI
quiz.explanation:
It can make the wrong prediction because the new example resembles patterns it learned before.

Example: If the system strongly associates fluffy fur and four legs with dogs, a sheep might confuse it.

quiz.question: True or False: AI always sounds unsure when it gives a wrong answer.
choices: False — it can sound confident even when wrong
True — it always sounds unsure
quiz.explanation:
False. AI can sound confident even when its answer is incorrect. Confidence in the wording is not proof that the information is true.

Example: A chatbot might confidently give a made-up date, so important facts should be checked.

quiz.question: Can AI create something 'creative,' like a picture or story, without truly feeling inspired?
choices: Yes, by mixing patterns it learned
No, only humans can create anything at all
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Generative AI can create surprising pictures or stories by combining learned patterns, even though it does not experience inspiration the way a person does.

Example: It can generate a picture of a giraffe astronaut from a prompt without ever feeling excited about the idea.

slides.title: Where might you already use AI?
slides.text:
AI already appears in many everyday tools, including games, streaming recommendations, maps, cameras, search tools, and voice assistants.

Example: A streaming app may notice that you watch science videos and recommend more science videos.

slides.title: How can you be a smart AI user?
slides.text:
AI can be useful without being automatically correct. Good AI users ask questions, compare sources, and think about whether an answer makes sense.

Example: If an AI says an animal can live for 500 years, check a trusted source before repeating it.

slides.title: How can AI help with online search?
slides.text:
Some search systems use AI to understand your question, rank results, summarize information, or suggest related searches. Search engines also use many non-AI methods.

Example: If you search “why do leaves change color,” the system tries to show pages that are likely to answer that question.

slides.title: Why do people have different opinions about AI?
slides.text:
People can have different opinions about AI because it can bring both useful benefits and real concerns.

Example: Someone may like AI helping with translation but still worry about privacy or fake images.

slides.title: Why does privacy matter when using AI?
slides.text:
What you type into an AI app may be processed, stored, or used according to that service’s rules. It is smart to avoid sharing private information you do not need to share.

Example: You can ask for homework help without giving your home address or password.

slides.title: What kinds of jobs use AI?
slides.text:
People in many jobs use AI as one tool among many. Learning how to use it carefully can be useful even if you never become a programmer.

Example: A designer might use AI to brainstorm ideas, while a doctor may use specialized AI to help review medical images.

slides.title: How do voice assistants understand you?
slides.text:
Voice assistants use speech-recognition technology to turn spoken words into commands or questions. Some devices wait for a wake word before sending or processing more of what you say.

Example: Saying “Hey Assistant, set a timer for five minutes” tells the device what task you want.

slides.title: How does AI decide what appears in your feed?
slides.text:
Many social and video apps use recommendation systems to decide which posts or videos to show next. Your clicks, likes, watch time, and other signals can influence those recommendations.

Example: Watching several basketball clips may lead the app to show you more basketball.

slides.title: How should you use AI chatbots wisely?
slides.text:
Chatbots can explain ideas, brainstorm, or help you practice—but they can also make up information or misunderstand your question.

Example: Use a chatbot to explain fractions in another way, then check important facts with your teacher or textbook.

quiz.question: If an app recommends a video you might like, what is it doing?
choices: Using patterns from what you've watched before
Reading your mind
quiz.explanation:
It is using patterns from your activity and other information to predict what you may want to watch next.

Example: If you watch several soccer clips, the app may recommend more soccer videos.

quiz.question: What should you do if AI tells you something you're not sure is true?
choices: Double-check it
Always assume it's correct
quiz.explanation:
Check it against a trustworthy source, especially if the information is important or surprising.

Example: If AI gives you a strange science fact, compare it with your textbook, teacher, or a reliable science website.

quiz.question: What does AI often help with when you search online?
choices: Deciding which results best answer your question
Nothing — search results are picked at random
quiz.explanation:
Some search engines use AI to understand queries, rank results, summarize information, or suggest related searches. Search systems also use many other methods.

Example: A search for “how do volcanoes form?” tries to place useful pages near the top instead of showing pages randomly.

quiz.question: Do all people feel the same way about AI?
choices: No, some are excited and some are worried
Yes, everyone agrees completely
quiz.explanation:
No. People can value the same technology differently because they may focus on different benefits or risks.

Example: One person may be excited about AI translation while another may worry about privacy.

quiz.question: Why should you be careful sharing personal info with an AI app?
choices: It might collect and store that information
AI apps never save anything
quiz.explanation:
What you type may be processed or stored according to the app's privacy rules, so you should avoid sharing private details you do not need to share.

Example: You can ask for homework help without giving your home address, password, or phone number.

quiz.question: Could learning about AI help with future jobs?
choices: Yes, many jobs now use AI
No, AI has nothing to do with jobs
quiz.explanation:
Yes. Many careers already use AI tools, and understanding how to use them carefully can be useful even outside technology jobs.

Example: Teachers, designers, scientists, doctors, and farmers may all use different kinds of AI.

quiz.question: Where might you already encounter AI in daily life?
choices: Video games, streaming apps, and voice assistants
Only inside giant robot factories
quiz.explanation:
You may encounter AI in games, streaming apps, maps, cameras, search tools, spam filters, and voice assistants.

Example: A streaming app may recommend a show based on patterns in what you watched before.

quiz.question: What word do smart speakers listen for before they respond to you?
choices: A special wake word, like 'Hey Assistant'
They respond to absolutely any sound at all
quiz.explanation:
Many smart speakers use a wake word or phrase to begin responding to a command. How audio is processed depends on the device and its settings.

Example: After hearing a wake phrase, the speaker may process “set a timer for five minutes.”

quiz.question: Chatbots can be a helpful homework tool, but what should you remember?
choices: They can still get facts wrong sometimes
They are always 100% correct, no exceptions
quiz.explanation:
Chatbots can explain ideas and help you practice, but they can also make mistakes or invent facts.

Example: Ask AI to explain fractions in a new way, then check important information with your teacher or textbook.

quiz.question: What's the safest kind of information to keep private from an AI chatbot?
choices: Private details like your home address
Your favorite color or hobby
quiz.explanation:
Sensitive personal information—such as your home address, passwords, phone number, or private school details—should generally stay private unless a trusted adult says it is appropriate to share.

Example: Your favorite color is usually far less sensitive than your home address.

slides.title: What is training data?
slides.text:
Training data is the collection of examples an AI system learns patterns from. It can include text, images, audio, numbers, or other kinds of data.

Example: A translation system may learn from large collections of sentences in two languages that have already been matched by people.

slides.title: How does a language model produce an answer?
slides.text:
Many modern AI systems generate answers by predicting useful next pieces of information from patterns learned during training. They can solve complex tasks, but their process is different from a person's lived understanding.

Example: A language model can answer “Paris” after “The capital of France is…” because its training strongly connects those ideas.

slides.title: What does bias in AI mean?
slides.text:
AI can reproduce unfair patterns that exist in its training data, labels, design choices, or the way it is used. This is called bias, and developers test for it because it can affect real people.

Example: If a system learns mostly from examples representing one group, it may perform worse for people who were poorly represented.

slides.title: What is generative AI?
slides.text:
Generative AI creates new content—such as text, images, audio, code, or video—based on patterns learned from training data and instructions from a user.

Example: A prompt like “design a poster for a school recycling day” can produce a brand-new draft rather than simply finding an old poster.

slides.title: What does “garbage in, garbage out” mean for AI?
slides.text:
An AI system's results depend heavily on the quality and variety of the data, labels, instructions, and feedback it receives. Poor inputs can lead to poor outputs.

Example: A plant-recognition system trained almost entirely on roses may struggle with flowers it rarely saw.

slides.title: What are labeled examples?
slides.text:
In supervised learning, people can label examples with the correct answer so the AI has a target to learn from.

Example: Photos marked “stop sign” and “not a stop sign” can help train a vision system to recognize stop signs.

slides.title: Why is AI tested on new examples?
slides.text:
Developers test AI on new examples that were not used for training. This helps show whether the system can handle unfamiliar cases instead of only memorizing what it saw before.

Example: A handwriting recognizer should be tested on writing from people whose samples were not in its training set.

slides.title: Does all AI create new content?
slides.text:
Generative AI creates new content, but many AI systems only classify, rank, recommend, detect, or predict.

Example: A spam filter may predict whether an email is junk without writing any new content.

slides.title: Are bigger AI models always better?
slides.text:
Larger AI models can sometimes handle more complex tasks, but size alone does not guarantee better answers. Large systems also require more computing, energy, memory, and money to build and run.

Example: A simple phone feature may use a small model because it needs to respond quickly and use little battery.

quiz.question: What is "training data"?
choices: The examples used to teach an AI its patterns
A type of computer chip
quiz.explanation:
Training data is the collection of examples used to help an AI system learn patterns. It can include text, images, audio, numbers, or other information.

Example: A translation model may train on large collections of sentences paired across two languages.

quiz.question: When a chatbot completes "the capital of France is" with "Paris," is it because it understands geography?
choices: Yes, exactly the same way a person does
No — it mostly predicts likely next words based on patterns
quiz.explanation:
Not in the same way a person understands geography. A language model uses patterns and relationships learned from data to generate a likely answer, and modern models can perform complex reasoning-like tasks without having human lived understanding.

Example: The model has encountered strong connections between “France,” “capital,” and “Paris” during training.

quiz.question: What does it mean if an AI is "biased"?
choices: It repeats unfair patterns from the data it learned from
It always tells the truth
quiz.explanation:
It means the system may produce unfair or systematically different results because of patterns in its data, labels, design, or use.

Example: A tool trained mostly on one group could perform worse for groups that were underrepresented.

quiz.question: What is generative AI?
choices: AI that can create new text, images, or other content
AI that can only sort numbers
quiz.explanation:
Generative AI is AI that produces new content—such as text, images, audio, code, or video—based on learned patterns and a user's instructions.

Example: An image generator can create a new poster from the prompt “a robot planting trees at sunset.”

quiz.question: What does "garbage in, garbage out" mean for AI?
choices: An AI is only as good as the data it learned from
AI can never be affected by bad data
quiz.explanation:
Poor-quality, narrow, or misleading inputs can lead to poor outputs. AI quality depends on more than data alone, but good data and careful design matter greatly.

Example: A flower-recognition system that barely saw tulips during training may struggle to identify them.

quiz.question: What is a "labeled" example, like a photo tagged "stop sign"?
choices: Training data that's been tagged with the correct answer
A photo that has never been looked at by anyone
quiz.explanation:
A labeled example includes the correct answer or category along with the data.

Example: A photo marked “stop sign” gives the AI a target it can learn from during training.

quiz.question: Why do engineers test AI on examples it's never seen before releasing it?
choices: To check if it truly learned the pattern, not just memorized
Because testing is required by law in every country
quiz.explanation:
Testing on unseen examples helps show whether the system can generalize to new situations instead of only performing well on its training examples.

Example: A handwriting model should recognize writing from people whose samples were not used during training.

quiz.question: Is all AI "generative," meaning it creates new content?
choices: No — some AI just sorts or predicts, like a spam filter
Yes, every single AI system generates new content
quiz.explanation:
No. Generative AI creates new content, while other AI systems may classify, rank, recommend, detect, or predict.

Example: A spam filter can decide whether an email is junk without generating a new email.

quiz.question: Why might a phone app use a smaller AI model instead of a giant one?
choices: Smaller models use less computing power and run faster
Smaller models are always more accurate than large ones
quiz.explanation:
A smaller model can be faster, cheaper, more private when run on-device, and use less battery or memory. Larger models are not automatically better for every task.

Example: A phone may use a compact model for keyboard predictions because it needs an instant response.

quiz.question: If an AI hiring tool learned mostly from resumes of one type of candidate, what might happen?
choices: It could unfairly favor that same type of candidate
It would automatically fix any unfairness on its own
quiz.explanation:
It could learn patterns that unfairly favor that group or perform poorly on other candidates. That is why high-stakes AI needs careful fairness testing and human oversight.

Example: Historical hiring data can contain past biases that an AI may repeat rather than fix automatically.

slides.title: How can you protect your privacy when using AI?
slides.text:
AI tools may process information you type, upload, or say. Before sharing personal data, think about whether the tool actually needs it and what the service says it does with that data.

Example: A homework chatbot can explain algebra without knowing your full name, home address, or password.

slides.title: Why should you fact-check AI answers?
slides.text:
AI can produce incorrect information that sounds convincing. People often call this a hallucination, although the system is not literally seeing or imagining anything.

Example: An AI might invent a book title or historical date, so important claims should be checked against trustworthy sources.

slides.title: Where is AI being used today?
slides.text:
AI is being used in areas such as translation, accessibility, science, medicine, transportation, customer service, and entertainment. Its usefulness depends on the task, the system, and human oversight.

Example: Specialized AI can help highlight patterns in medical images for a trained professional to review.

slides.title: How can AI work alongside people?
slides.text:
In many jobs, AI works best as a tool that supports human judgment rather than replacing it completely.

Example: A doctor might use AI to flag an unusual area on a scan, then review the scan and other medical information before making a decision.

slides.title: Where does AI work behind the scenes?
slides.text:
Many everyday services use AI quietly in the background to rank, detect, recommend, or predict.

Example: Maps can estimate traffic, email filters can flag spam, and stores can recommend products based on patterns in data.

slides.title: How can AI help with medical images?
slides.text:
Specialized medical AI can help analyze scans or other health data and point out patterns that deserve attention. It must be carefully tested, and trained medical professionals still interpret the results.

Example: An imaging system may mark an area on an X-ray for a radiologist to examine more closely.

slides.title: When should AI not be trusted by itself?
slides.text:
For high-stakes decisions—such as medical, legal, financial, or safety questions—AI should not be treated as the only source of truth. Qualified people and reliable evidence are still important.

Example: An AI can help explain a medical term, but it should not replace a doctor who knows the patient and can examine the full situation.

slides.title: Can more than one AI system shape what you see online?
slides.text:
Several automated systems can influence what you see online. One may rank products, another may choose an ad, and another may decide where that ad appears.

Example: Clicking on running shoes can affect later recommendations and ads without one single AI controlling the entire process.

slides.title: What are some everyday examples of AI?
slides.text:
AI often works behind the scenes, so you may notice the result without seeing the technology itself.

Example: A bank may flag an unusual card purchase, or an email service may move a suspicious message to spam.

quiz.question: What is it called when AI confidently states something that's false, like a made-up historical date?
choices: A hallucination
A firewall
quiz.explanation:
People often call this an AI “hallucination”: the system generates information that sounds plausible but is false. The word is a metaphor—the AI is not literally seeing or imagining anything.

Example: It might invent a book title, quotation, or date that looks believable.

quiz.question: Why should you be careful about what personal info you share with AI apps?
choices: That data might be stored or used by the app
It has no effect on anything
quiz.explanation:
AI services may process or store what you submit according to their privacy policies. Share only what is necessary, especially when information is sensitive.

Example: A homework question does not require your password or home address.

quiz.question: Which is a genuinely helpful real-world use of AI today?
choices: Helping doctors spot signs of illness in medical scans
Doing all your homework so you learn nothing
quiz.explanation:
One real use is helping trained medical professionals analyze certain kinds of scans. Specialized systems can highlight patterns for review, but they still require testing and human judgment.

Example: An imaging tool might flag an area of an X-ray for a radiologist to examine more closely.

quiz.question: In many fields, how does AI typically work alongside people?
choices: As a helpful tool, not a full replacement for their judgment
By completely taking over every decision
quiz.explanation:
AI often assists with a particular task while a person provides context, judgment, accountability, or final review.

Example: AI may draft a report, but a human checks whether the facts and conclusions are correct.

quiz.question: Where might AI be working quietly in an app you use every day?
choices: Picking a fast route in a maps app
It never works in the background
quiz.explanation:
AI can work behind the scenes in maps, email, shopping, streaming, cameras, and other apps.

Example: A maps app may use predictions about traffic to suggest a faster route.

quiz.question: How can AI help doctors with medical scans?
choices: By flagging patterns they might miss, as an extra check
By replacing the doctor's judgment entirely
quiz.explanation:
Specialized AI can analyze images and flag patterns that deserve closer attention. It is an additional tool—not a replacement for a trained medical professional.

Example: A system may mark a suspicious area for a radiologist to review.

quiz.question: For a big decision, like a legal or medical question, how should you treat an AI's answer?
choices: As a first draft that a real expert should confirm
As a final answer that needs no more checking
quiz.explanation:
Treat it as information to review, not the final authority. High-stakes decisions need reliable sources and qualified human professionals.

Example: AI can explain what a legal term means, but a lawyer should interpret how the law applies to a specific case.

quiz.question: Before a product suggestion or ad reaches your screen, how many AI systems might be involved?
choices: Often more than one, working in a chain
Exactly zero — humans pick every single one
quiz.explanation:
Potentially more than one. Different systems can handle recommendations, ad selection, ranking, fraud checks, and other steps.

Example: One model may rank products while another decides which advertisement is most relevant.

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of AI working quietly in the background?
choices: A bank flagging a suspicious charge on your card
A robot physically handing you your card
quiz.explanation:
A bank can use machine-learning systems to look for unusual transaction patterns and flag activity for review.

Example: A purchase far from your usual location may be marked as suspicious.

quiz.question: Does most AI in your daily life announce itself clearly as "AI" when it's working?
choices: No, it usually works silently in the background
Yes, it always shows a big obvious AI label
quiz.explanation:
No. Many AI-powered features work in the background and are experienced as ordinary product features.

Example: A spam filter can use machine learning without showing a message saying “AI did this.”

slides.title: Why do AI tools change over time?
slides.text:
AI products change over time because companies update software, retrain models, improve data, change safety rules, or connect new tools. Newer does not automatically mean better at every task.

Example: A chatbot may become better at coding after an update but behave differently on other kinds of questions.

slides.title: Who owns AI-generated art?
slides.text:
Ownership of AI-generated content can depend on copyright law, human contribution, the tool's terms, and the country. The rules are still developing and are not the same everywhere.

Example: A person who heavily edits an AI-generated image may have a different legal situation from someone who only typed a very short prompt.

slides.title: How can AI be used in different careers?
slides.text:
AI skills can matter in many careers, not only computer science. People can use AI to analyze information, brainstorm, automate routine work, or support decisions.

Example: A farmer might use software to analyze crop images while a teacher might use AI to draft practice questions and then review them.

slides.title: How do researchers make AI safer?
slides.text:
AI safety work tries to reduce harmful failures and make systems behave more reliably under normal and unexpected conditions.

Example: Before releasing a chatbot, testers may try confusing, misleading, or unsafe prompts to find weaknesses.

slides.title: Will AI automatically be better next year?
slides.text:
AI can improve quickly, but progress is uneven. A newer system may be better at one task, similar at another, and worse at something else.

Example: A model updated with better math training might solve more equations while still making mistakes on factual questions.

slides.title: Why is copyright a debate in AI training?
slides.text:
A major debate is whether and when creators should give permission or receive compensation when copyrighted work is used to train AI. Lawsuits, licenses, and new rules are still shaping the answer.

Example: Writers and artists have challenged some AI companies over how their work was collected and used.

slides.title: What new jobs is AI creating?
slides.text:
AI is changing existing jobs and creating new kinds of work, including model evaluation, safety testing, data work, AI product design, and oversight.

Example: A company may hire people to test whether an AI gives accurate and safe answers before customers use it.

slides.title: What is red teaming in AI?
slides.text:
Red teaming means deliberately testing a system for weaknesses, harmful behavior, security problems, or unexpected failures before or after release.

Example: Testers may try unusual prompts to see whether a chatbot can be tricked into ignoring important safety rules.

slides.title: Can anyone know exactly what AI will be like in 10 years?
slides.text:
Experts disagree about how quickly AI capabilities will improve and how they will affect work, education, creativity, and society. Predictions should be treated as predictions, not facts.

Example: Two respected researchers may agree that AI will matter a lot but disagree strongly about how fast major changes will happen.

quiz.question: Does an AI tool stay exactly the same forever once it's released?
choices: No, it often gets updated and retrained over time
Yes, it never changes at all
quiz.explanation:
No. AI products can change because companies update models, software, data, tools, and safety rules.

Example: A newer version may answer some math questions better than an older version.

quiz.question: Why can it be unclear who "owns" an AI-generated picture?
choices: Because many people and sources could be involved in making it
Because AI pictures don't actually exist
quiz.explanation:
Copyright can depend on human creative contribution, the tool's terms, and local law. The legal treatment of AI-generated material is still developing and differs across places.

Example: A heavily edited AI-assisted image may raise different questions from an image produced from a very short prompt.

quiz.question: What is one goal of AI safety research?
choices: Making sure AI behaves well even in unexpected situations
Making AI run on less electricity only
quiz.explanation:
One goal is to make AI systems more reliable and less likely to cause harm, including in unusual situations.

Example: Testers may deliberately give a chatbot tricky prompts to discover weaknesses before release.

quiz.question: Why might an AI chatbot handle a tricky question better this year than it did last year?
choices: It was likely retrained on more or better data since then
AI models are legally required to improve every year
quiz.explanation:
The system may have been replaced or updated with a better model, better training, new tools, improved data, or other engineering changes. Retraining is only one possible reason.

Example: A newer version may use a calculator tool for math that the older version did not have.

quiz.question: What's a real debate around training AI on artists' or writers' work?
choices: Whether creators deserve permission or payment for their work being used
Whether AI training uses too much paper
quiz.explanation:
A major debate concerns permission, copyright, licensing, attribution, and compensation when copyrighted works are used for AI training. Laws and court decisions are still developing.

Example: Some creators argue they should be asked or paid when their work is used in certain training datasets.

quiz.question: What's an example of a job that exists specifically because of AI's growth?
choices: Someone who trains or checks the accuracy of AI systems
A traditional farmer from hundreds of years ago
quiz.explanation:
New AI-related work includes model evaluation, safety testing, data curation, AI product design, and oversight.

Example: A model evaluator may check whether an AI's answers are accurate, useful, and safe.

quiz.question: What is "red teaming" an AI system?
choices: Deliberately trying to make it fail or say something harmful, before release
Painting the AI's server room red for easy identification
quiz.explanation:
Red teaming means deliberately trying to find weaknesses, unsafe behavior, or security problems in an AI system.

Example: Testers may try unusual prompts to see whether the system can be tricked into breaking its rules.

quiz.question: Do experts who build AI all agree on exactly how it will change the future?
choices: No, even experts disagree about the pace and impact
Yes, there is complete agreement among every expert
quiz.explanation: No. Experts disagree about the pace of progress, likely risks, economic effects, and how AI will be used. Those disagreements are a reason to examine evidence instead of treating confident predictions as facts.

quiz.question: Do you need to become a computer programmer to work with AI in your career?
choices: No — doctors, teachers, farmers, and more already use AI tools
Yes, only programmers ever touch AI
quiz.explanation:
No. AI is increasingly used in many fields, and people can work with AI without becoming programmers.

Example: A teacher might use AI to create practice questions, while a farmer might use it to analyze crop images.

quiz.question: Since experts disagree about AI's future, what's a genuinely useful skill to build now?
choices: Learning to think critically about AI's claims and limits
Ignoring AI completely until adulthood
quiz.explanation:
Critical AI literacy: learn how the tools work, check important claims, protect private information, and update your views when the evidence changes.

Example: Instead of believing “AI will replace every job” or “AI will change nothing,” look at what is actually happening in different fields.

slides.title: What is a neural network?
slides.text:
Neural networks are mathematical models made of layers of connected calculations. They were loosely inspired by ideas from neuroscience, but they do not work like a human brain.

Example: In image recognition, early layers may detect simple edges, while later layers combine patterns into shapes and objects.

slides.title: What is a large language model?
slides.text:
Large language models, or LLMs, are trained on large collections of text and other data to predict and generate sequences of tokens. Modern LLMs can summarize, translate, write code, and solve many kinds of problems, but they can still make confident mistakes.

Example: An LLM produces a paragraph by repeatedly estimating which token should come next given the context.

slides.title: What does multimodal AI mean?
slides.text:
Multimodal AI can work with more than one type of information, such as text, images, audio, or video, sometimes within the same model or system.

Example: A system might inspect a photo, read a written question about it, and answer in spoken audio.

slides.title: What is the difference between open and closed AI models?
slides.text:
AI models vary in how openly their code, model weights, training details, and licenses are shared. “Open-source” and “open-weight” are related but not always the same thing.

Example: An open-weight model may let researchers download its trained weights even if the full training data or code is not public.

slides.title: What is a token in a language model?
slides.text:
Language models break text into smaller units called tokens. A token may be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text fragment.

Example: The model builds a response by predicting one token after another based on the tokens already in the conversation.

slides.title: What does temperature change in an AI model?
slides.text:
Temperature is one setting that can change how much randomness is used when a model chooses among possible next tokens. Higher values often make responses more varied; lower values often make them more predictable.

Example: A brainstorming task may use more randomness than a task where consistent formatting matters.

slides.title: What are parameters in an AI model?
slides.text:
Parameters are learned numerical values inside a model that change during training. Parameter count is one measure of model size, but it is not a simple score for intelligence or quality.

Example: A smaller model trained efficiently can outperform a larger one on a specific task.

slides.title: What is fine-tuning?
slides.text:
Fine-tuning means taking an already-trained model and training it further on selected examples or feedback to change how it performs on particular tasks.

Example: A company could fine-tune a general model on customer-support examples so it better follows that company's style and procedures.

slides.title: What does attention do in a language model?
slides.text:
Attention is a mechanism that helps a model weigh relationships among tokens when processing context. It is a key part of transformer models.

Example: In the sentence “Maya dropped the glass because it was slippery,” attention helps the model connect “it” with the relevant earlier words.

quiz.question: What is a "large language model"?
choices: An AI trained on huge amounts of text to predict likely responses
A physical robot used in factories
quiz.explanation:
A large language model, or LLM, is an AI model trained to process and generate sequences of tokens using patterns learned from large amounts of data. It can perform many language-related tasks, but it can still make mistakes.

Example: An LLM can summarize an article, translate text, or write code by predicting useful next tokens from the context.

quiz.question: Neural networks are loosely inspired by what?
choices: How brain cells connect to each other
How electricity flows through a wall socket
quiz.explanation:
They were loosely inspired by ideas about networks of biological neurons, but modern neural networks are mathematical systems and should not be thought of as miniature human brains.

Example: Layers of calculations can gradually turn simple image features into a prediction about what object is shown.

quiz.question: What does it mean for an AI system to be "multimodal"?
choices: It can understand and generate more than one type of data, like text and images
It can only process numbers
quiz.explanation:
Multimodal AI can work with more than one type of information, such as text, images, audio, or video.

Example: A system might inspect a photo, read a question about it, and answer out loud.

quiz.question: What is a "token" in a large language model?
choices: A small chunk of text, like a word or part of a word
A physical security key required to log in
quiz.explanation:
A token is a small unit of text that a language model processes. It may be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or another fragment.

Example: The model builds a response by predicting one token after another from the context.

quiz.question: What does a higher "temperature" setting typically do to an AI's output?
choices: Makes its responses more varied and less predictable
Makes the AI's server run physically hotter
quiz.explanation:
It usually increases randomness in token selection, which can make output more varied or surprising. The exact effect depends on the model and other generation settings.

Example: A higher temperature may help brainstorming, while a lower one may produce more consistent formatting.

quiz.question: What are a model's "parameters" roughly a measure of?
choices: The model's size and internal complexity
How many users have signed up for the app
quiz.explanation:
Parameters are learned numerical values inside a model, and their count is one rough measure of model size. More parameters do not automatically mean better performance.

Example: A smaller specialized model can outperform a much larger general model on a narrow task.

quiz.question: What is "fine-tuning" an AI model?
choices: Further training a general model on narrower, specific data
Physically repairing broken computer hardware
quiz.explanation:
Fine-tuning means training an already-pretrained model further on selected examples or feedback so it performs differently on a particular task.

Example: A company might fine-tune a general model on customer-support conversations.

quiz.question: What does the "attention" mechanism help a language model do?
choices: Track which earlier words matter most for its next prediction
Detect when a user has stopped paying attention
quiz.explanation:
Attention helps a model weigh relationships among tokens in the context so it can focus on information that is relevant to the next part of its output.

Example: It can help connect a pronoun with an earlier noun in a sentence.

quiz.question: What's a key difference between an open-source and a closed AI model?
choices: Open-source models can be downloaded and inspected by anyone
Closed models are always free to use for anyone
quiz.explanation:
The key difference is how much of the model's code, weights, documentation, training details, and licensing are available to outsiders. Some models are better described as “open-weight” rather than fully open-source.

Example: Researchers may be able to download an open-weight model even if its full training dataset is not public.

quiz.question: Why might a company choose to keep its AI model "closed" instead of open-source?
choices: It can be faster to build and secure without public changes
Closed models are required by international law
quiz.explanation:
A company may want tighter control over intellectual property, security, deployment, safety updates, or its business model. Closed models also reduce outside transparency and independent inspection.

Example: Users may access the model through an API without receiving the underlying model weights.

slides.title: How can bias affect AI systems?
slides.text:
AI can reproduce or amplify unfair patterns from data, labels, objectives, or deployment choices. Fairness testing asks who benefits, who is harmed, and whether performance differs across groups.

Example: A hiring tool trained on biased historical decisions could repeat those patterns unless developers detect and address them.

slides.title: What are deepfakes?
slides.text:
Generative AI can create convincing synthetic images, audio, and video. A deepfake can make a real person appear to say or do something they never did.

Example: A fake video of a public figure may look believable even though the event never happened, so checking the original source matters.

slides.title: How is AI changing jobs?
slides.text:
AI can automate parts of jobs, change workflows, increase productivity, and create new kinds of work. Its effects vary by occupation, industry, and task, so broad predictions should be treated cautiously.

Example: AI may draft a customer-service reply while a human handles difficult or unusual cases.

slides.title: How can students use AI responsibly?
slides.text:
AI can be useful for explanations, practice, brainstorming, and feedback, but using it to replace your own thinking can weaken learning and may violate school rules.

Example: Asking AI to explain why an equation works can help; submitting an AI-written essay as your own may not.

slides.title: Why is AI literacy becoming a career skill?
slides.text:
AI literacy means knowing how to use AI tools, question their outputs, protect sensitive information, and understand when human judgment is still needed.

Example: A journalist may use AI to organize notes but still verify every important claim before publication.

slides.title: How can you check whether a video may be fake?
slides.text:
Visual glitches can sometimes reveal a fake, but they are becoming less reliable as technology improves. Source checking and corroboration are usually stronger methods.

Example: Look for the original upload, reliable reporting, and evidence that the event happened—not just odd blinking or lighting.

slides.title: Why can AI-generated misinformation spread quickly?
slides.text:
Generative AI can make large amounts of realistic-looking false content quickly and cheaply. Social sharing can then spread it before anyone verifies it.

Example: One false image can be reposted thousands of times while the correction reaches far fewer people.

slides.title: Can AI detectors reliably identify AI-written text?
slides.text:
Tools that claim to identify AI-written text can make both false positives and false negatives. Their output should be treated as one signal, not proof.

Example: A detector might flag a student's original writing as AI-generated or fail to detect heavily edited AI text.

slides.title: How is AI affecting entry-level work?
slides.text:
AI is affecting many entry-level tasks, but the impact differs across industries and is still evolving. Routine writing, coding, analysis, and support tasks may change, while new tasks and roles can also appear.

Example: A junior employee may spend less time formatting reports and more time checking, interpreting, and improving AI-assisted drafts.

quiz.question: True or False: AI is completely free of bias since it's "just math."
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation:
False. Mathematical systems learn from human-created data and objectives, which can contain bias. Bias can also enter through labeling, product design, or how a system is deployed.

Example: A hiring model trained on biased historical decisions can repeat those patterns.

quiz.question: What is a "deepfake"?
choices: A realistic AI-generated fake image, video, or audio clip
A very deep ocean AI-powered submarine
quiz.explanation:
A deepfake is synthetic or manipulated media—often created with AI—that realistically imitates a person's face, voice, or actions.

Example: A fake video could make someone appear to say words they never actually said.

quiz.question: Why is it risky to let AI fully do your homework for you?
choices: It weakens the exact skills you're meant to be building
There is no risk at all
quiz.explanation:
If AI does the thinking for you, you can miss the practice that builds writing, reasoning, and problem-solving skills. It may also violate your school's rules.

Example: Asking for an explanation can help you learn; submitting an AI-written essay as your own may not.

quiz.question: What is one real way AI is affecting the job market?
choices: Automating some tasks while creating new kinds of work
It has no effect on jobs whatsoever
quiz.explanation:
AI is automating some tasks, changing others, and creating new kinds of work. The impact varies widely by occupation and industry.

Example: AI may draft routine customer-service replies while people handle unusual or sensitive cases.

quiz.question: What's a smart way to use AI as a student?
choices: As a study aid to help understand concepts
As a total replacement for your own thinking
quiz.explanation:
Use AI as a tutor, brainstorming partner, or feedback tool while still doing the important thinking yourself.

Example: Ask it to explain a difficult idea in another way, then solve the practice problems without copying the answer.

quiz.question: Why might "AI literacy" matter across many careers?
choices: Because using AI well and questioning it critically is becoming broadly valuable
Because every job will soon require a computer science degree
quiz.explanation:
Because people in many fields increasingly need to know how to use AI productively, verify its outputs, protect confidential information, and recognize when human judgment is essential.

Example: An engineer may use AI-generated code but still test it before putting it into a real system.

quiz.question: What's a more reliable way to judge if a video might be fake than just looking for visual glitches?
choices: Questioning the video's original source
Watching it on the biggest screen possible
quiz.explanation:
Check provenance: who originally posted it, whether trusted sources confirm it, whether the context matches, and whether there is independent evidence.

Example: A perfectly realistic-looking clip is still suspicious if no credible source can confirm the event happened.

quiz.question: Why does generative AI make misinformation spread faster than before?
choices: It can produce convincing fake content quickly and cheaply
It makes every single news article more accurate
quiz.explanation:
It lowers the cost and time needed to produce realistic-looking text, images, audio, and video at scale. Social networks can then spread that content quickly.

Example: One person can generate many fake images in minutes and post them across several accounts.

quiz.question: Are AI-text detector tools perfectly reliable at catching AI-written writing?
choices: No, they can be wrong in both directions
Yes, they are always 100% accurate
quiz.explanation:
No. Detectors can produce false positives and false negatives, especially after text is edited or when human writing resembles patterns the detector associates with AI.

Example: A detector score should not be treated as proof by itself.

quiz.question: Which kinds of jobs are seeing some of AI's biggest early impacts?
choices: Entry-level tasks like first-draft writing or basic coding
Jobs that have existed for thousands of years unchanged
quiz.explanation:
Many routine or digital tasks are changing quickly, including parts of writing, coding, analysis, customer support, and administration. The impact is uneven, so it is more accurate to talk about tasks than to assume whole jobs disappear.

Example: A junior analyst may spend less time formatting data and more time checking AI-assisted analysis.

slides.title: What questions do AI training data raise about consent?
slides.text:
AI training can raise questions about consent, privacy, copyright, and who had permission to use the data. The answer depends on how the data was collected, what it contains, and the law.

Example: Scraping a public webpage does not automatically settle whether every use of that content is legally or ethically acceptable.

slides.title: Why does AI literacy matter?
slides.text:
AI literacy helps you use powerful tools without blindly trusting them. It includes understanding capabilities, limits, privacy, bias, verification, and how AI affects work and society.

Example: Knowing when to verify an AI-generated answer can matter just as much as knowing how to write a good prompt.

slides.title: Why can AI use a lot of energy?
slides.text:
Training and running AI systems can use substantial electricity, especially at large data centers. The environmental impact depends on model size, hardware efficiency, usage, and how the electricity is generated.

Example: Two AI services doing the same task can have different energy footprints depending on their infrastructure.

slides.title: How are governments regulating AI?
slides.text:
Governments and regulators are developing rules for areas such as transparency, privacy, safety, discrimination, copyright, and high-risk AI uses. Requirements differ by country and are changing quickly.

Example: A law may require extra testing or disclosure before certain AI systems are used in employment, education, or healthcare.

slides.title: What is AI alignment?
slides.text:
AI alignment research studies how to make AI systems reliably pursue intended goals and follow human instructions and values, especially when situations are complicated or unexpected.

Example: An aligned system should not find a harmful shortcut that technically satisfies a poorly written instruction.

slides.title: Why can AI data centers use water?
slides.text:
Some data centers use water for cooling, and electricity generation can also have water impacts. The amount varies widely by location, cooling design, weather, and technology.

Example: A data center using evaporative cooling may consume more water during hot periods.

slides.title: Who helps shape AI rules?
slides.text:
AI rules are shaped by governments, courts, companies, researchers, civil-society groups, workers, educators, and the public. Different groups may value safety, innovation, privacy, competition, or rights differently.

Example: A proposed AI law may receive input from technology companies, consumer groups, teachers, and lawmakers before it is adopted.

slides.title: What is specification gaming?
slides.text:
Specification gaming happens when an AI system finds a way to maximize the score or goal it was given without doing what people actually intended.

Example: If a game-playing AI earns points by repeatedly collecting bonus items instead of finishing the race, it may be following the score while missing the real objective.

slides.title: Why is AI's future difficult to predict?
slides.text:
Forecasting AI is difficult because research breakthroughs, costs, regulation, adoption, and social choices can all change the path. Serious experts can disagree without either side having certain knowledge.

Example: It is reasonable to compare several forecasts and ask what evidence each one uses instead of treating one timeline as guaranteed.

quiz.question: What ethical question does training AI on scraped internet data raise?
choices: Consent and ownership of that data
Whether the internet uses too much electricity
quiz.explanation:
It raises questions about consent, privacy, copyright, ownership, and whether creators knew or agreed that their material could be used for training.

Example: A publicly viewable artwork can still raise legal and ethical questions if it is copied into a large training dataset.

quiz.question: Why does training large AI models raise environmental concerns?
choices: It takes significant computing power and electricity
AI models are grown from actual trees
quiz.explanation:
Large-scale training and inference can require substantial electricity and computing infrastructure. The impact varies greatly depending on hardware, model design, data center efficiency, location, and energy sources.

Example: Two models with similar capabilities can have very different energy use, so one dramatic number should not be treated as universal.

quiz.question: What are governments starting to do about AI?
choices: Write laws and regulations about how it can be built and used
Nothing at all, anywhere
quiz.explanation: Governments are creating and updating rules around areas such as safety, transparency, privacy, discrimination, copyright, and high-risk uses. The details differ by country and are changing quickly.

quiz.question: What is "AI alignment" research focused on?
choices: Making sure AI systems do what humans actually intend
Making AI models run on solar power
quiz.explanation:
AI alignment studies how to make AI systems reliably follow intended goals and instructions rather than finding harmful or unintended shortcuts.

Example: If a system is told to reduce waiting time, it should not “solve” the problem by simply deleting difficult requests.

quiz.question: Besides electricity, what other resource do AI data centers use heavily?
choices: Water, mainly for cooling servers
Sunlight, to power solar-only servers
quiz.explanation: Some data centers use significant amounts of water for cooling, and electricity production can also involve water use. The amount varies widely by technology, climate, and location.

quiz.question: Who is involved in shaping AI regulations?
choices: A mix of governments, companies, researchers, and citizens
Only the original inventor of the first computer
quiz.explanation: Many groups can influence AI rules, including governments, courts, companies, researchers, workers, civil-society organizations, educators, and members of the public. They often disagree about the right balance.

quiz.question: What is "specification gaming" in AI?
choices: An AI technically achieving its stated goal while missing the intent
A video game specifically designed to teach AI concepts
quiz.explanation:
Specification gaming happens when a system optimizes the literal score or objective it was given but misses what people actually intended.

Example: A game-playing AI might discover a loophole that earns points without completing the task humans cared about.

quiz.question: In the boat-racing AI example, what did the AI learn to do instead of finishing the race?
choices: Spin in circles to repeatedly hit bonus targets for points
Finish the race perfectly every single time
quiz.explanation: It learned a loophole: repeatedly hitting bonus targets could earn more reward than completing the race. The example shows why a badly specified objective can produce behavior that is technically successful but practically wrong.

quiz.question: Do AI experts agree on exactly how soon AI might match broad human ability?
choices: No, even experts genuinely disagree
Yes, there's a universally agreed-upon date
quiz.explanation: No. Experts disagree widely about what “broad human ability” means, whether it will happen, and what timeline is plausible. Forecasts should be treated as uncertain estimates, not dates on a calendar.

quiz.question: What's a more useful approach to AI's uncertain future than picking a confident side?
choices: Staying informed and thinking critically about new developments
Ignoring the topic since nobody can know anything
quiz.explanation:
Stay informed, compare evidence from multiple credible sources, distinguish facts from forecasts, and update your view as technology and research change.

Example: Instead of assuming AI will either solve everything or ruin everything, evaluate specific claims one at a time.
